summary:
BOWIE – the friend who flies with you.
Sol 257 on Mars. It’s 3 a.m., you can’t sleep, and the people you love are ten light-minutes away. On the ISS, astronauts see a flight psychologist every two weeks. On Mars, there is no live call home. Bowie is a learning robot companion that lives on board: it gets to know its astronaut before launch, checks in every day through simple conversation, reads the body’s signals against a personal baseline, learns what actually helps, and knows when it’s time to bring in humans. Fully offline. Named after my dog, because some things should come with you, no matter how far you go.
details:
Sol 257.
The habitat is quiet. Your heart rate variability has dropped for three days. You slept five hours. Your answers have been getting shorter: “Fine.” “Tired.” “No.” Nobody notices, because everybody is tired. Earth is almost ten minutes away at the speed of light, and the next private call with your psychologist is still days out.

Bowie notices.

The problem. NASA names five hazards of human spaceflight. Three of them, isolation, confinement and distance from Earth, attack the mind as much as the body. Today, ISS crews talk to a flight psychologist every two weeks and call home whenever they want. On a Mars mission, that safety net turns into delayed messages. Most health software watches the body. Almost nothing is built for the part that breaks quietly.

Meet Bowie. A 3D robot dog that becomes a crewmate.

It gets to know you before launch. Not with a form, but with a conversation: who is waiting for you at home, why you’re going, what helps when it gets hard, how others can tell when you’re struggling, and how you want to be talked to.

It listens, every day. Two minutes. One question that feels like small talk (“How did you feel when you woke up?”), but each one quietly maps to an item of the WHO-5, a validated well-being index from the World Health Organization. Bowie estimates how you’re really doing without ever handing you a questionnaire.

It reads your body, and connects it to your mind. Heart rate, HRV, sleep, blood oxygen and temperature are compared to your normal, not a population average. “Your HRV is 18% below your normal. Stress shows up in your heart too.” Rising temperature plus heart rate? It suggests rest and alerts the medical officer. A mission radiation tracker uses real dose rates measured by NASA’s Curiosity rover against the NASA 600 mSv career limit.

It learns what helps you. Breathing, music, a message home, a game night with the crew: after every suggestion you say if it helped, and Bowie adapts with a simple, transparent learning rule. Week by week it knows you better.

It knows where it is. Live Earth–Mars signal delay from an orbital model, the current mission phase, and early signs of “psychological closing”, when isolated crews start saying less and less.

It never pretends to be human. Several hard days, worrying words or body warnings always lead to people: the crew, the medical officer, the flight psychologist. Bowie prepares a summary for the next conference, and the astronaut decides whether it is sent.

Why a dog? Because I have one. His name is Bowie. He doesn’t fix my problems, but he notices when something is off, and he is always there. On the longest journey humans have ever planned, astronauts deserve that too.

Bowie runs fully offline, keeps all data on board, explains every reaction with visible rules, and is honest about what’s real and what’s simulated.

The body gets you to Mars. The mind gets you home.
